title: Trump's AI Safety Agency Chief Resigns After Three Months as Indian-Origin Arvind Raman Takes the Helm
excerpt: Chris Fall's abrupt departure from CAISI marks the third leadership upheaval at the federal AI testing body since January, with former Purdue engineering dean stepping in as acting director.
body:
• Chris Fall has resigned as director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) just three months after his appointment
  • Arvind Raman, an Indian-origin academic and former dean of engineering at Purdue University, will serve as acting director
  • Fall's departure marks the third leadership disruption at the AI testing body under the Trump administration
  • The resignation comes amid White House efforts to restrict the agency's public evaluations of frontier AI models

The head of the federal government's primary AI testing and evaluation body has resigned after just three months on the job, the Commerce Department confirmed on Sunday.

Chris Fall stepped down as director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), the unit within the Department of Commerce responsible for evaluating frontier AI models before their public release. Arvind Raman, an Indian-origin academic who leads the Commerce Department office overseeing CAISI, will serve as acting director, a department spokesperson told Reuters.

Raman is the former dean of engineering at Purdue University, one of the top engineering programs in the United States. His appointment places an Indian-origin scientist at the helm of one of the most consequential technology policy bodies in the federal government at a moment of intense global debate over AI governance.

A Pattern of Leadership Turmoil

Fall's departure marks at least the third leadership disruption at the AI testing body since President Trump took office in January. In April, a former Anthropic researcher was forced out of a CAISI leadership position within days of starting, reportedly because of the administration's ongoing feud with the AI developer. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick subsequently restructured the body, renaming it from its Biden-era title, the AI Safety Institute.

The revolving door reflects a deeper tension within the administration over the government's role in AI oversight. White House AI advisers, including venture capitalist David Sacks, have warned that excessive model verification could slow deployment and hamper economic growth, according to the Wall Street Journal. Others within the government view CAISI as essential to maintaining U.S. leadership in AI safety standards.

Public Evaluations Under Pressure

The resignation follows a period of increasing restrictions on CAISI's public-facing work. Last month, the Wall Street Journal reported that White House officials instructed the agency to stop publishing its AI model evaluations — reports that had served as independent benchmarks for the industry.

“This agency is capable of sophisticated testing and has relationships with leading companies.”

— Chris Lehane, OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer

A new executive order, signed in June, created a voluntary framework for AI companies to submit frontier models for government review up to 30 days before release. Critics say the order effectively assigned CAISI's existing work to a new body while restricting the agency's ability to share its findings publicly. Companies will still submit models for review, but the results will largely stay behind closed doors.

OpenAI had publicly called for CAISI to be strengthened with more resources and responsibilities. Major AI companies including Anthropic and Google have maintained working relationships with the agency dating back to the Biden administration.

An Indian-American at the Crossroads of AI Policy

Raman's elevation comes at a moment when Indian-Americans hold an outsized role in U.S. technology leadership. As dean of Purdue's College of Engineering from 2017 to 2023, he oversaw one of the largest engineering programs in the country — a school known for producing a significant number of Indian-origin tech leaders across Silicon Valley and beyond.

The AI policy decisions made under his watch could have far-reaching implications for the global tech industry. CAISI is expected to continue evaluating AI models internally and working with other government agencies, but its future scope and public role remain uncertain. The Commerce Department has not announced a timeline for naming a permanent replacement for Fall.

What's Next

The agency's instability raises fundamental questions about whether the United States can maintain credible AI oversight while the technology advances at an unprecedented pace. Other nations, including the EU with its AI Act and the UK with its AI Safety Institute, have moved to establish more permanent regulatory frameworks.

For now, the immediate challenge falls to Raman: steadying an agency that has been buffeted by political winds while preserving its working relationships with the companies whose models it is supposed to evaluate.
